(p-151) Sūrat al-ʿAlaq (The Clot)

It is also called *Iqraʾ* (Read).

Its principal theme is the command, especially to worship the One to whom belong creation and command, out of gratitude for His favour, in avoidance of ingratitude toward Him, out of hope for His Gardens and fear of His Fires, because it is established that He will requite the servants on the Day of Return. Each of its two names indicates this, because the Sustainer is owed gratitude and His denial is to be utterly forbidden. Moreover, *Iqraʾ* points to the command, and *al-ʿAlaq* points to creation. *Iqraʾ* indicates the beginning, which is worship, by direct denotation (*muṭābaqa*), and the end, which is salvation on the Day of Religion, by necessary implication (*luzūm*). *Al-ʿAlaq* indicates both the end and then the beginning by inclusive implication (*iltizām*), because whoever knows that he was created from a clot knows that his Creator is able to restore him from dust, since dust is more receptive to life than blood. Whoever believes in the return acts for it. He specified the clot because it is the composition of life, and for this reason it was called a soul.

*Bismillāh*: "In the name of God," who possesses the attributes of perfection and thus deserves exclusive divinity. *Al-Raḥmān*: whose blessing is universal, and therefore deserves gratitude from all creatures. *Al-Raḥīm*: who granted success to whomever He willed (p-152) from among His elect, by bestowing upon them noble gifts and abundant bounties.

* *

When He, glorified and exalted, commanded him in *al-Ḍuḥā* to speak of His blessing, and reminded him of its comprehensive forms in *Alam Nashraḥ* (Q. 94:1), this produced his singling out with what He commanded him in its conclusion: specifying Him alone with desire. Thus in *al-Zaytūn* He indicated that He is worthy of this, by the completeness of His power, which necessarily implies that no one else has power except through Him. This produced the completeness of wisdom, which yielded with certainty the resurrection for recompense. The listener thus became eager for what would bring about a good recompense on that Day, and by what means one stands before the Supreme King on the Great Day of Gathering, from among the qualities of those who believed and did righteous deeds. So He guided to this in this sūrah, beginning with an introduction to the primary knowledge, mentioning the origin of him whom He created, glorified and exalted, in the best stature, and some of his states, both good and bad, as a marvel at the completeness of His power, glorified and exalted, and as an alert to recognise them and to contemplate them attentively. He placed the verb governing the prepositional phrase first here, because it has a stronger effect upon the soul, since it was the first to be revealed, so the command to read was the more important: ﴿Read﴾. Its object is omitted, as a sign that there is no reading except of what He commanded him to read, which is the great Whole, so the meaning is: bring about reading of that which has no readable other than it, namely the Qurʾān, which comprises every good. He made clear to him that he cannot do this except with the help of God, who educated him and perfected his education, and reared him and perfected his upbringing. So He said what guided the meaning to its implied sense: while you are beginning the reading ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, that is, by saying the basmalah, or seeking help from the One who has been good to you, by His Most Beautiful Names and Sublime Attributes, through what He has specially granted you in (Q. 94:1), or by mention of His name. The intended meaning in this case of "name" is the Sublime Attributes, and it was expressed thus because the goodness of the name implies the goodness of what it signifies, and the exaltation of the name implies the exaltation of the one named and all that he is described by and attributed to. They said: this indicates that reading is not complete except with the invocation of the name. Because it is in the context of a command to obedience, which calls to it by recalling blessings, He did not mention the Greatest, all-comprehensive Name, and He mentioned the attribute of goodness by nurture, which encompasses what is other than it, and as a comfort to him, peace be upon him, because it was the first revelation, at the time when solitude was made beloved to him, so he would withdraw alone, worshipping his Lord in the cave of Ḥirāʾ. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him with the first five verses of this sūrah, up to His saying ﴿what he did not know﴾ (Q. 96:5). For this secret He drew it in the manner of the basmalah, with an expression that is more comforting at the beginning of the matter and broader than it. So He pointed to the Greatest Name by the attributes of perfection contained in the whole discourse, and He pointed to the generality of the favour of the All-Merciful by the attribute of creation, whose generality is indicated by omitting the object, and to the particularity of the attribute of the All-Compassionate by the (p-153) nobility which is of its nature to reach its ultimate end. That cannot be without the outpouring of work that pleases, so it becomes a cause for lasting honour, and by teaching which by its nature guides to good pleasure. He pointed to seeking refuge by the command to recite the Qurʾān, because of what His saying, glorified and exalted, implies: ﴿And when you recite the Qurʾān, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ (Q. 17:45) [that is, of the devils of mankind and jinn] ﴿a concealed barrier﴾ (Q. 17:45), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ (Q. 16:98).

When He specified him, by attributing this noble description to him as an honour, He described Him in general terms as the Creator and the Commander, to inform that He has the governance and the influence. He began with creation because it is perceptible by the eye, so it is more firmly fixed in understanding, closer to conception, and more indicative of existence, of great power, and of perfect wisdom. So beginning with it in this sūrah, which is the first revealed, was the most appropriate matter, because the first of obligations is knowledge of God, and this is in the utmost clarity with regard to His acts. So He said: ﴿Who created﴾. Omitting its object indicates that this attribute belongs to Him: determining and bringing into existence in accordance with the determination now and in what will be. Everything that enters existence is therefore from His making, and it oscillates between His permission and His prevention, His harm and His benefit.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 2:

(p-155) Since the animal is the most perfect of created beings, and man is the most perfect of animals, the cream of its churning, the essence of its reality, and the pure core of its nature, and since he is the strongest indication of the perfection of power, being a comprehensive gathering of everything in the cosmos, his creation was more wondrous than the creation of others. For this reason he is a greater indication of the perfection of the Creator and of the obligation to single Him out in worship. He singled him out, saying: ﴿He created man﴾, that is, this species, of which it is natural to be at ease with its own kind and with what its character, senses, and the fellow members of its species have become accustomed to.

Since the Arabs used to eat blood, and God, exalted is He, had forbidden it because it is the origin of man and of the other animals, and it is the compound of life, so that whoever eats it takes on the nature of that which is its blood, He said, informing that He, glorified and exalted is He, built this abode upon the wisdom of causes, although He is able to create without gradual causation, saying: ﴿from a clinging clot﴾, that is, [He created] this kind from this thing, which is blood, intensely red, solid and thick. It is called ʿalaqah in the singular, and likewise the clay that clings to the hand is called ʿalaq. They all acknowledge that the human being was created from both of these. Therefore the verse is one of the proofs of our Imam al-Shafiʿi, may God be pleased with him, for the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its meanings. Perhaps he expressed it thus so that it would include clay, and so it would be—along with what it contains of allusion to the wondrous craftsmanship—an allusion to the prohibition of eating what is our origin, of blood and dust, before it transforms. Then, (p-156) when it transforms, it is described as lawful (ḥalāl), because transformations have a bearing on what is made lawful, in marriage and otherwise. The reddening of the sperm-drop is not a transformation, because it was red before the desire restrained it, and perhaps when desire weakened from restraining it, it descended [red]. When the blood turns into flesh, it passes into the category of what is lawful. Likewise, when dust turns, through mixing with water, into a date or a grain, it becomes lawful.

Imam Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr said: When God, glorified and exalted is He, said to His Prophet ﷺ, ﴿So what makes you deny the Judgment after this?﴾ [al-Tin: 7] ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8], the meaning of that was: what thing has prompted this in you after the matter has become clear to you and explained? He, glorified is He, has declared Himself free of denying the reckoning and has exalted His station above that. But the path of such a statement, when it comes, is like the path of His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Him, your deeds will surely be voided﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and its category. The ruling of this kind is clear with respect to whoever is addressed by the address and is actually intended by it from his community ﷺ, in view of their lack of infallibility and the possibility that doubts and suspicions may reach them. So the sense of the speech is: what thing could possibly make you hesitate or deny the matter of the reckoning, when what removes doubt and dispels confusion has become clear to you? Do you not know that your Lord is the most just of judges? Would it befit Him, who is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, to make the variation of your states in (p-157) doubts after He created you in the best of forms? Would it be becoming for Him to do that in vain? God has said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27]. When God, glorified and exalted is He, established for the servants that He is the most just of judges, together with what preceded that by way of the requirement of negating doubt concerning the kind of truth, if one considers and reflects, and the Surah of al-ʿAlaq came in the order, indicating that by which healing occurs, and from which one learns the beginning and the end, namely His Clear Book, which God, exalted is He, made an elucidation of all things, a guidance, a mercy, and good news for the doers of good, He commanded its recitation so that they might reflect upon its signs. So He said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], seeking help through Him, and then your path will become clear and your guide will be made manifest. ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. Also, He, exalted is He, made His servants most knowledgeable of His creation of man in the best of forms, ﴿then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5], and there resulted from him, as has been explained earlier, the divergence of the two extremes and the difference of those who speak, all of it by His prior wisdom and will: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13]. God, glorified is He, has made clear to us the furthest end that the most honored of His creatures and the most exalted of His servants with Him attains from the human species. That is what the two surahs before this have made clear concerning the state of our Prophet, the Chosen one ﷺ, and His great and generous promise to him in His saying: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5]. And the excellence of the state at the beginning of ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1], following the request ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ [Ta-Ha: 25], up to what the verses of the two surahs indicated of his distinguished characteristics. That is the highest station that anyone of those mentioned attains. So the sequence of that was followed by a surah (p-158) that contained an allusion to the state of whoever was placed in the other extreme of the human species. That is the state of the one referred to from the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen him who forbids﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 9], ﴿a servant when he prays﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 10], up to His saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 19], so that the difference of the two ranks and the contrast between the two states would appear. This is the customary practice in books. The explicit definition did not occur here as it occurred in the other extreme, so as to match the intended meaning. Perhaps some who has not perceived this will object here that this surah is among the very first revealed, so how does your aim of claiming its arrangement after what was revealed later hold true? We say to him: Where has your objection gone regarding a number of surahs preceding it, indeed most of them? Otherwise, the Surah of al-Baqarah is not among the Medinan ones, and the requirement of our composition, by building the surahs after it on the arrangement found in the Mushaf of the community, is in fact upon it, and in it there is a distance from the Meccan that cannot be counted. What has escaped you is forgetting what we mentioned in the introduction, that the order of the surahs in which they are is due to the action of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, whether that was by revelation from him or by the ijtihad of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, as we have mentioned. So return your gaze, review your consideration of the introduction, and may God grant us success in considering His clear signs and reflecting upon His verses, and lead us in that to what brings us near to Him by His bounty and grace. Ends.

Once He, glory be to Him, had completed what He willed regarding the creation, namely bringing things into existence [through causes] (p-159) gradually, He began to draw attention to the realm of command (ʿālam al-amr), which is origination (al-ibdāʿ) without causes. He said, repeating the command to read, to indicate the greatness of this matter, to console him (ﷺ), to calm his fear, and to inform him that the one who came to him with the command before him is not like their lords: ﴿Read!﴾ Since he (ﷺ) had said at this command, as a statement of fact, what the state of his condition says even without speaking with the tongue of speech, "I am not a reader," the implied meaning was: "Your Lord, who nurtured you and made your upbringing good, and disciplined you and made your discipline good, commanded you to read, and He is able to make you a reader." He joined to this, [his saying]: ﴿And your Lord﴾, meaning that the sense is: "And the state is that He who singled you out with abundant favour is ﴿the Most Generous﴾," that is, the one who possesses the greatest perfection absolutely, in His essence, in His attributes, and in His actions, so that no deficiency whatsoever attaches to Him in any respect at all. For His reality is far removed from blame and combines all the noble qualities, and He is the one who combines the highest excellences of character, and no other is described by this. He gives you what cannot be encompassed by enumeration. He indicated that among this is that He pours out upon his unlettered community knowledge and fortune in a measure He did not pour out upon any community before it, despite the shortness of their lifespans. So He said, pointing to knowledge and teaching, and implying by His description, glory be to Him, as the Giver of knowledge, the arrangement of the ruling of His being the Most Generous upon this attribute, which transports the human being from the lowly intellectual state (p-160) to this exalted and perfect state.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 4:

﴿Who taught﴾ meaning: after the forbearance (ḥilm) toward them in not hastening to punish them with torment and retribution, out of generosity (jūdan) from Him, without any impediment arising from fear of consequence or hope of benefit. ﴿By the pen﴾, meaning: writing by means of it.

Nazm al-Durar of al-Biqa'i, on surah 96, verse 5:

When He alerted, by this, to the benefits of writing, which none but Him, glorified and exalted is He, can encompass, because the affairs of religion and worldly life, in this world and the Hereafter, are founded upon it, and it is sufficient as an indication of the subtle wisdom of the Exalted and the delicate nature of His management, He increased that greatness in a way that embraces others, so He said: ﴿He taught﴾, that is, the knowledge both necessary (ḍarūrī) and acquired by reflection (naẓarī) (ḍarūrī and naẓarī), ﴿man﴾, that is, the one whose nature is to be at ease with what he is in, who does not move on to other than it, rather he forgets it unless his Lord inspires it in him, ﴿what he did not know﴾, that is, by His subtle kindness and wisdom, so that his condition is ordered in his religion, from the Book and the Sunnah, and in his worldly life, from transactions and crafts. Thus He pours upon him from His knowledge of the divine kind (ʿilm ladunnī), whose apparent cause is not known, by which one knows the arrangement of premises through the terms of the major and minor (ḥudūd wa-wusṭā), so that he knows conclusions, and by which one knows intuitive matters (ḥadsiyyāt). This is after the creation of faculties, the establishing of proofs, and the sending down of signs. Had it been by means alone, people would have been equal in the duration of learning and in the basis of what is known, as they are equal in the duration of gestation and the basis of humanity. He, glorified is He, has mentioned the beginning and end of man by transferring him from the lowliest states to the highest, affirming His lordship and establishing His bounty of honour.

(p-161) Al-Mallawi said: "Had any of the gifts and blessings been more noble than knowledge, He would have mentioned it right after the attribute of bounty (al-akramiyya)." End of quotation. In that is an indication of the increased generosity of scholars through teaching. In the verse is also an indication to contemplating the two worlds, that of creation and that of command. Al-Razi said: "In each of the two worlds there is particularity and generality." End of quotation.

So the meaning is that He teaches you, O Noble Prophet, even though you are unlettered and at present know nothing, just as He taught by the pen one who did not know. Thus you, by what the attribute of bounty indicates, despite your unlettered state, are more knowledgeable than the people of the pens, and higher than every lofty station.

Since blood is the most abundant of the humours (al-akhlat, the four bodily humours) and the most violent in its agitation, its disease resembles none of the diseases of the remaining humours. Yet it is also quick to heal if its cure is correctly obtained and it is treated with a overpowering remedy stronger than itself. Knowledge is, for the most part, a companion of wealth, and the slip of a scholar exceeds the slip of others. Al-Biqa'i said, making known, after introducing the divine matters (al-Ilahiyyat), the matter of the soul, clarifying the state of the human being who is returned to the lowest of the low, establishing his condition, and deterring him from his error: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: let the learned one desist from transgression if he truly attains wealth. ﴿Indeed, man﴾, meaning: this kind, which is your kind, and whose nature is to be at ease with himself and to look upon his own self ﴿surely transgresses﴾, meaning: it is in his nature, except for those whom Allah, glorified is He, protects, to exceed the limit which he should not pass, just as blood increases the blood humour. He emphasized it because of the majority of creation's denial of it, for no transgressor admits that he has transgressed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 7:

﴿An﴾, that is, because ﴿he sees himself﴾, that is, the human being knows himself ﴿'ilman wujdaniyyan﴾ (an experiential, intuitive knowledge) ﴿as self-sufficient﴾, that is, he finds richness for himself. This is the predominant disposition of the human being: whenever he becomes self-sufficient regarding something, he becomes blind to the places of his need, his conditions change with him, and he oversteps in it what he ought to stop at. "Nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust." Whoever is in need of something is submissive to it, as in the hadith of the last of the people of the Fire to exit it, who swears to his Lord that he will not ask for anything other than what he has sought. When You give it to him and he becomes self-sufficient through it, he asks for something else, until he enters the abode of permanence. Perhaps by this he alerted that this needy nation will be granted the treasures of the earth, and wealth will make it transgress, as it made those before it transgress, even though they deny that, as the Prophet ﷺ said when he gave them the good news of the conquests, and said: "Indeed, a platter will be brought to one of you in the morning and another in the evening." Then he said to them: "Are you today better, or on that day?" They said: "Rather on that day, we will be free for the worship of our Lord." He said: "Rather you today are better than you on that day." The Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, it is not poverty that I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out over you as it was spread over those before you, so you will compete for it as they competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them."

Or as the Prophet ﷺ said.

Since there is no remedy for this (heedlessness) like remembering the recompense, He said, making known that man never ceases to be in need of his Lord (Mawlā) in his life and in his death, and in his wealth and his poverty, warning him of the evil of his states, and emphasizing (it) because of their denial of that: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who has been good to you with the Message by which He raised your mention, not to other than Him, such as dust and the like, ﴿is the return﴾, i.e., the greatest return, the established one from which there is no escape. As for in this world, there is no escape from acknowledging it, for no one has power over anything except by His decree. As for the Hereafter, (it is) by what He established in His proof in Surah al-Tin, so He will call people to account for their deeds and recompense each person with what he deserves of reward or punishment. Therein is a warning to the transgressor [and a belittling] of a wealth that will come to an end.

When He had informed of his transgression, He hastened to mention its remedy, because hastening to the remedy, lest the disease take hold, is obligatory. He indicated his transgression with a warning of the consequences of the return (al-ruj'a), in the style of interrogation (taqrir), because it is more striking to the soul and more awe-inspiring to the intellect. For Abu Jahl said: "If I see Muhammad prostrating his face in the dust, I will surely crush his head with a rock." So he came to do what he claimed, but he turned back on his heels and his hands became stuck to his waist. He was asked what had befallen him, and he said: "Indeed, between me and him there is a terror and wings." In another narration: "A trench of fire." In another narration: "A stallion camel. I have never seen the like of it, and had I come near him, it would have devoured me." The origin of this hadith is in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), [who said]: ﴿Have you seen﴾ It has already been mentioned in al-An'am (p-164) that this verb, when it is not visual, carries the meaning of "informed" (akhbara). So the meaning is: [inform me], have you known with your heart a knowledge that is as clear as the sight of your eye ﴿him who forbids﴾, that is, in the sense of renewal and continuity.

Since the most abominable thing is that which turns a servant away from serving his master, He said, expressing it in terms of servitude, denying any exaggeration in the reprehensibility of the prohibition and indicating the perfection of servitude: ﴿a servant﴾, i.e., one of the servants, ﴿when he prays﴾, i.e., serves his Master, whose lordship no one can deny, by performing the prayer (ṣalāh), which is his connection to Him. It is the greatest kind of worship, for although it is the closest connection to the Truth, it is also a complete severance and withdrawal from creation. So his forbidding him from this was a forbidding him from rendering the right to its people, out of envy or insolence. This indicates that it is the nature of [the people of] every age to be hostile to the people of virtue and to bar them from good, lest they be singled out for perfection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 11:

When this was a matter beyond bounds in transgression, and the question was only about seeing his state in forbidding the servant from prayer, not about seeing his essence, the listener became eager to know that [state], so the statement was repeated with added amazement at his condition and warning. He said, repeating the operative word for additional emphasis and to clarify that this is in reality the first part of the question about the state: ﴿Have you seen﴾, meaning, tell me about his condition ﴿if he is﴾, meaning this forbidder, ﴿upon guidance﴾. He used the particle of elevation (ʿalā, "upon") to indicate that he is in the utmost firmness and establishment, so He said: ﴿upon guidance﴾, meaning perfect (p-165) in guidance, so that he would withdraw from forbidding this worshipper from serving his Lord, whose lordship he acknowledges even if he falsely claims that He has a partner, just as he does not forbid prostration to idols.

And when he (al-Biqa'i) had mentioned what might be upon him in perfecting his own self, he mentioned what he might suffer in rescuing others, so He said: ﴿Or enjoins﴾, i.e., that forbidder, ﴿piety﴾, i.e., which is the pillar (ʿimad) of the religion, and it is the cultivation of the inner self with the light arising from guidance, and the cultivation of the outer self for that, springing forth from the cultivation of the inner self, which necessitates it. So he enjoins this worshipper to persist in serving his Master, who is agreed upon in His lordship, and there is no doubt about His unity in lordship, by turning toward what pleases Him of acts of worship, so that this will be a protection for the doer from His wrath, and he will be safe from perdition. The answer is omitted, its estimated meaning being: Would it not be better for him? So let him reflect upon every matter of his affairs, and not proceed with it until he knows by evidence that it is guidance and piety.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 13:

Since the implied meaning was necessarily as the context indicates, namely the answer to the two questions that you have supplied, he built upon it his saying, as an increase in rebuke, reproach and censure, a question about the state of this forbidder, which contradicts the first state, repeating the verb to clarify that: ﴿Have you seen﴾, that is, tell me, O listener, and do not hasten. ﴿If he denies﴾, that is, [caused] this forbidder to commit denial, in that the one who prays is upon guidance (al-Hudā) by serving his master, whose lordship is agreed upon (p-166). He thereby commits error, which is undoubtedly error, and nothing calls to it except guidance.

Since the denier [has] not ceased from his lying, he pointed out that this person's state is other than that, so he said: ﴿and turns away﴾, that is, and he imposed upon his original fitra (innate nature) after treating it, turning away from accepting the command to piety. That turning away is the ruin of the inner self through the bad character traits arising from denial, and the ruin of the outer self through the ugly deeds arising from denial. The answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: Was that turning away and denial not an evil for him? Because denial and turning away without evidence are pure evil, so how much more so when the evidence stands against both of them.

When he (al-Biqa'i) marvelled at this man's state, which is far removed from reason both in regard to himself and in regard to his fellow human beings, he rebuked him with a question that expressed wonder at the fact that he knows that nothing is in his hand, the one who produces (the outcome), because he is watched and his condition is controlled to the utmost degree of control, and yet he forgets this. So he said, mentioning the second object of ﴿أَرَأَيْتَ﴾ ("tell me"), which can only be a question clause: [﴿Did he not know﴾] meaning: there occurs for him some action on one of the days, [﴿that Allah﴾] meaning: He is the Supreme King, [﴿sees﴾] meaning: [for Him] are the attributes of sight and knowledge in an absolute sense, so He knows every thing known and sees every thing seen. Whoever has this attribute is deserving that He destroy whoever sees him upon misguidance and leading others astray, and that He grant victory to whoever obeys His command against everyone who opposes him. This rebuking interrogation came in this manner because they acknowledge everything that is denied to them in it, and it necessitates for them, [by what they do], from enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), that they be deniers of him, and that is the very contradiction than which nothing is more abominable in their view. This is one explanation; it is also possible, and it is the better one, that the verse be understood as ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted from each of two parallel parts, and each part's omission is supplied by the other), so it is said: since the question concerned the condition of the one who forbids, because the seeing is a seeing of knowledge and not of sight, the listener became eager to know it, and the one who forbids had two conditions: obedience and disobedience. It began with the first, because of its nobility over the other, in the form of a past-tense affirmation expressed as wonder, so he said: ﴿Tell me﴾, meaning: inform me, ﴿if he﴾ (the one who forbids) is firmly established in his prohibition, being steadfast, ﴿upon guidance﴾, meaning the perfect guidance, ﴿or﴾ he had been ﴿enjoining﴾ in that command, or in some command, of worshipping idols and other things, ﴿righteousness﴾. He omitted the answer to the question about this condition because the answer to the second condition indicates it, and that answer is: ﴿Did he not know that Allah sees﴾ every thing that can be seen, so He forbids it if it is disliked, does not approve of it, and holds him accountable for it, so that this one who forbids may weigh his actions by what He, glorified be He, has prescribed of rational and revealed proof, and thus know whether they are of what pleases Him, so that He may approve them for him as He approves [all] that pleases Him, or whether they provoke His anger, so that He prevents him from them.

When he had mentioned what the condition of the one who forbids could be of rectitude, he mentioned what could be of corruption in it, so he said, affirming, expressing wonder, and repeating the governing verb to intensify the wonder, in the same pattern as the first: ﴿Tell me, if he denies﴾, meaning this one who forbids, in truth, at the time of the prohibition. And since denial does not necessarily entail ﴿turning away﴾ he said: ﴿and turns away﴾, meaning from the religion by this prohibition of his. Thus he was firmly established in misguidance and desire in such a way that [he] does not produce any act except a corrupt one. ﴿Did he not know that Allah sees﴾, so that he would hold himself accountable by the proofs to which He, glorified be He, has guided, and know that what he is upon of right guidance, if Allah approves it for him and enables him to do it, or of error, if He forbids him from it and does not approve it for him, as He did with this one who swore: "I will surely crush the head of this worshipper," and advanced upon him with his rock, while he, in his own estimation, was at the utmost power to do so by his own claim, but Allah prevented him from it and turned him back, so he returned on his heels, humbled, with cowardice, terror, and other things visible upon him, of the kind that men shun and that the bravest lions disdain. The ihtibak here, with the verb ﴿Tell me﴾ as a clause, is not a case of tanazu' (grammatical contention between two verbs for one object), because that would require an ellipsis of a pronoun, and clauses are not elided in that way; rather it is of the type of omission for a known reason. So the omission of "being upon misguidance" in the second part is because of the indication of "being upon" in the first part, and the omission of "Did he not know that Allah sees" in the first part is because of the indication of its mention at the end.

[p-169]- Since this wretch turned away from this knowledge, which he acknowledges entirely, and his turning away was only due to the portions and desires that he has, which bring him down by the judgment of being returned "to the lowest of the low" to the rank of beasts, He brought the greatest of the tools of deterrence and said: ﴿Nay!﴾ That is, he has no knowledge of anything of that, because his rank is lower than the rank of beasts, and nothing of anything is in his hand. Thus he has no power over anything of what he aimed at of harm. Let him therefore desist from pursuing that, for he harms only himself.

Since denying knowledge of him might suggest that he is among the heedless, for whom there is no blame, He made clear that the absence of knowledge in him is not due to heedlessness, for which its possessor is excused. Rather, it is due to neglect of good and contentment with blindness and imitation. He is thus of the category of the astray, who squandered the use of the cognitive faculty mentioned in al-Fatihah. So He resumed informing about him in answer to one who says, "What will be done with him?" He expressed it with the particle of contingency, to place him and others in the position of hope that he will cease, preserving the obligation, and He emphasized it because they were deniers: ﴿If he does not desist﴾, that is, if this forbidding one does not devise against this obedient servant, so that he stops and refrains from what he is engaged in of his prohibition, his denial, and his turning away.

Since the matter did not require more than emphasis for the occurrence of the act, He expressed it in its literal form and did not transfer it into a metaphor, indicating that this forbidder is too insignificant to need a severe act against him. Rather, the least breath of punishment suffices for his destruction. The purpose of emphasis was only to comfort the hearts of the friends and to refute the enemies. So He said: [p-170] ﴿We will surely seize﴾, that is, by God, we will certainly take and grip with a grip and seizure, with severity and violence, along with dragging, pulling, slapping, pushing, and fury, like the seizing of one who bites what he seizes, humiliates it, blackens its face, and defiles it, ﴿by the forelock﴾, that is, by the hair at the front of the head, which is its most noble part. The Arabs do not disdain anything as they disdain seizing the forelock. If the sanctity of the most noble is violated, then what of other than it? He dispensed with an annexation by the definiteness of prior reference.

When it was known that whoever is seized in this humiliating and degrading state is doomed, he dispensed with saying "and We will drag him by it on his face into the Fire." He described it with what indicates that, saying, substituting (*badal*, a substitute or apposition, a description that brings it closer to definiteness): ﴿a forelock﴾, meaning greatly ugly; ﴿lying﴾, meaning deliberately lying; ﴿sinful﴾, meaning that from it proceeds sin, including lying and other things, without intention. Most of its states are [other than] correct, sometimes deliberately and sometimes not deliberately. This is only because of the bad disposition (*jibillah*) of its owner, to the point that hardly any sound action proceeds from him. Describing it with what belongs to its owner, by metaphorical attribution (*isnad majazi*), is an intensification in denying that he has any power to prevent the one who is guided or to humiliate him or to inflict any harm on him, except if the Lord of the whole affair permits him in what would be a cause of increasing the other's elevation. In departing from the literal expression, as if it were said "the forelock of a liar, a sinner," together with this metaphor, there is a grandeur, majesty and sublimity that is not hidden. (p-171)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 17:

Since this is the utmost humiliation, and the disbelievers, in their arrogance, pride and sense of might, aim only to avoid becoming followers and tails (of others), and their might lies only in their people, and the closest thing a person takes pride in is his people of the assembly (nādī), namely the folk who gather by day so that some of them may converse with others and find comfort in one another's company, because of the sincere friendship among them, since they do not abandon their occupations by day and gather for that purpose except for that reason. God, Exalted is He, said, causally linking it to His seizing them in this degrading manner: ﴿Then let him call upon his assembly﴾, that is, a call for help (istighāthah), ﴿his assembly﴾, that is, [the people] who used to gather with him by day, conversing in a place where some call out to others among their helpers and clan, so that they may rescue him from what he is in. The one about whom this was revealed is Abu Jahl. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Do you threaten me? I am the one with the most people in the valley to call upon.»

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 18:

As if it were said: "If he called his council (nādiyahu), what would happen?" He said: ﴿We will call﴾, meaning by a promise that admits no breaking, ﴿the guards of hell (al-Zabaniyah)﴾, meaning the agents assigned to the Fire to drag him into it. Originally they are called *al-Shurṭ* (the police). The singular is *zabaniyah*, like *Hibriyah*, from *al-zabn*, which means pushing away, or *zabaniyy* by the relative form, whose original is *zabānī*, with the *tā'* as a substitute for the *yā'*. They are every being whose creation is huge and whose assault is severe. The Uthmanic codices (*al-maṣāḥif al-ʿUthmāniyyah*) agreed on deleting the *wāw* from this [verb] as an error, and there is no reason in Arabic for deleting it in pronunciation. (p-172) It seems that the meaning in this, and God knows best, is that one should not suppose they were called for some elevation of their own essences by which they would be aided, because the meaning of the *wāw* according to the *Rabbāniyyīn* (divine scholars) is height and elevation. This is an indication that they have no strength except through the Strong, the Mighty. Or it may be said that the deletion signals that the verb resembles the imperative, to show that this calling is a matter that must certainly take effect, and that the called ones must answer what they are called to, and that all of this occurs with the utmost firmness and coherence between its writing and its meaning and its order. This is especially so with the emphasis by the *sīn*, which indicates the certainty of unity and establishment. Or the meaning may be: We call them with the easiest call and the simplest command, and from them comes what cannot be endured and whose repelling cannot be achieved in any way. So how much more if We reinforced their calling and strengthened their resolve.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 96, verse 19:**

Since what preceded was the forbidding of the one who forbids the worshipper, and the threat of the forelock being seized if he does not desist, and the command to call upon his assembly, and since the ruling in the first case is that He does not respond to him by abandoning prayer, and in the second that the one who forbids does not desist from his disobedience through threat, and that the call of his assembly does not benefit him, then all of this is negated. It is most fitting, in the fullest sense of fitness, to use the particle of restraint, so He said: ﴿No!﴾, meaning: he is not able to call upon his assembly, nor does he desist from harming the obedient one by threat. So let him be restrained from all of that.

Since it was as if it were said, "Then what should I do?", He said, making known that whoever knows that the nature of the time and its people is corruption, it is obligatory for him to turn toward his own affair and to turn away from the rest of the servants: ﴿Do not obey him﴾, meaning in his prohibition to you from obedience, through prayer or otherwise.

Since his prohibition concerned prayer, which is the pillar of the religion, and since prayer is expressed by prostration (sujud), because prostration, although it is a part of prayer, is its most noble part, and because it is also applied to worship in general, He said, Exalted is He, indicating the victory for him (ﷺ) and his followers over everyone who prevents them from worshipping: ﴿And prostrate﴾, meaning: persist in your prayer and humble yourself with your soul, and renew that at every time. Since prostration is the closest that a servant comes to Allah, He said: ﴿and draw near﴾, meaning: strive with your inner self to reach the degree of nearness to your Lord and to win His love through every act of worship, especially prayer, for the servant is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating. This station has been explained, as was mentioned in al-Fatihah, by his (ﷺ) saying: "I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your punishment." This phrase conveys, as the Imam al-Ghazali said in the Book of Gratitude (Kitab al-Shukr), only the witnessing of Allah's acts. It is as if he saw nothing but Allah and His acts, so he sought refuge in His act from His act. He said: Then he drew near, and passed away in the witnessing of states, and ascended to the sources of acts, which are the attributes, so he said: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath," and these are two attributes. Then he saw that as a deficiency in tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness), so he drew near and ascended from the station of witnessing the attributes to the witnessing of the Essence, so he said: "And I seek refuge in You from You," fleeing from Him to Him, without seeing act or attribute. Yet he saw himself as fleeing from Him to Him, and seeking refuge and praising, so he passed away from witnessing himself. When he saw that as a deficiency, he drew near and said: "You are as You have praised Yourself; I cannot number praise of You." So his saying "I cannot number" reports the annihilation of his self and his departure from witnessing it, and his saying "You are as You have praised" is a declaration that He is the one who praises and the one who is praised, and that all things originate from Him and return to Him, and that everything perishes except His Face. Thus the beginning of his station was the ultimate end of the stations of the monotheists (muwahhidun), which is that none is seen except Allah and His acts, so he seeks refuge in an act from an act. Look, then, to where his ultimate end arrived when he reached the One, the Real, until there was removed from his sight and witnessing anything other than the Real Essence. Indeed, he (ﷺ) never ascended from one rank to another without seeing the earlier one as distant in comparison with the later one, so he would seek Allah's forgiveness for the earlier, and regard that as a deficiency in his conduct and a shortcoming in his station. To this refers his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed, a veil comes over my heart, so that I seek Allah's forgiveness in a day and a night seventy times." That was because of his ascent to seventy stations, some of which are reckoned a deficiency compared with their earlier ones, even though he was passing beyond the furthest limits of the stations of creation. Yet it was a deficiency in comparison with the later ones, so this was the reason for his seeking forgiveness.

When 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Allah has forgiven you your earlier and later sins; so what is this weeping in prostration and this severe exertion?" He said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" Its meaning: Should I not be seeking increase in the stations, for gratitude is the cause of increase, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. End of quotation.

This, as you see, is of great preciousness. Whoever increases in supplication in his prostration is likely to have it answered for him. Prayer is not but by recitation. When you do that, you are veiled from the others by a strong veil, you increase in purity, and you guard your state from the other, as is indicated by what is in the Scrolls of Abraham, upon him be prayer and peace: "It behooves the intelligent person to be guardian of his tongue, aware of his time, and devoted to his own affair." And Allah knows best. Thus its last part returns to the first, in the best manner, most beautiful and most complete. And Allah is the Guide.
